tension: Early warning vs. signal noise | Centralized escalation vs. distributed authority
summary: Set up early warning systems that detect when your business is straining, then respond quickly and proportionally. Keep everything aligned and functioning.

title: Catching Problems Before They Hurt
tension: Compliance as burden vs. compliance as living stewardship
summary: Keep your facility safe by inspecting regularly, maintaining equipment properly, and training people to handle emergencies. When you spot issues early and fix them, fewer accidents happen.

title: Catching Problems Early and Responding Fairly
tension: Maintaining rule compliance without concentrating enforcement power or destroying the social fabric that makes the commons worth protecting
summary: Watch for rule-breaking, respond proportionally, and bring people back in line—without tearing the community apart or harming the ecosystem.

title: Catching Rain Together
tension: Treating water as hidden pipes vs. treating water as visible commons infrastructure; seasonal abundance vs. year-round scarcity; individual property rights vs. collective retention responsibility.
summary: Communities design streets, farms, and buildings to capture seasonal rains and share water security—turning climate adaptation into visible, shared infrastructure everyone maintains.

title: Catching When Assets Lose Value
tension: Fidelity to current reality vs. resistance to acknowledging loss and impairment
summary: Spot when shared assets are declining in real time so you can act quickly and honestly before problems compound. Truthful accounting keeps everyone's trust.

title: Changing APIs Without Breaking Things
tension: System evolution vs. consumer stability: the need to change vs. the need to rely
summary: How to evolve your APIs and databases safely—keeping old systems working while introducing new capabilities, so your partners don't get blindsided.

title: Check In With Your Values Regularly
tension: Intention vs. Drift: The gap between what we say matters and where our time, energy, money, and attention actually flow widens silently until crisis forces recognition.
summary: Set up simple review rhythms (weekly, quarterly, yearly) to see where your life matches what you actually care about, catch drift early, and adjust course before small gaps become big problems.

title: Check Who Pays and Who Benefits
tension: Concentrated decision-making vs. distributed accountability | Hidden externalities vs. visible trade-offs
summary: Before any major decision, assess who bears the costs and who gains. Only renew policies if communities confirm the benefits are shared fairly.

title: Checking If You Live Your Values
tension: Espoused values vs. embodied practices — the slow, invisible drift that accumulates until identity fractures or harm compounds silently
summary: Regularly compare what you say you believe with what you actually do—catch the drift before it becomes a problem, and decide consciously whether to adjust your actions or rethink your values.

title: Checking If Your Life Matches Your Values
tension: Intention vs. Reality — the gap between who you claim to be and how your systems actually allocate energy, resources, and impact.
summary: Regularly examine how you actually spend your time, money, and attention to see if it aligns with what you say you care about and whether you're contributing to the commons or just taking from it.

title: Checking Someone Before You Hire
tension: Speed vs. Trustworthiness — the need to onboard quickly without concealing risks or enabling harm
summary: A fair way to verify who someone is and whether they're trustworthy, using references, background checks, and clear records that anyone can question.

title: Checking Your Thinking
tension: Implicit mental models (invisible, defended, calcified) vs. Explicit, tested, evolving frameworks (alive, transparent, adaptive)
summary: Regularly examine the invisible assumptions that shape how you see the world. Surface blind spots, refresh outdated beliefs, and build shared understanding across different perspectives.

title: Choosing a Legal Form That Fits
tension: Legal structure as constraint vs. legal structure as enabler of mission fidelity
summary: Your legal structure shapes how decisions get made and who controls them. Pick one that actually reflects how you want to operate, not just what looks good on paper.

title: Choosing the Right Trees for Your City
tension: Monoculture vulnerability vs. adaptive genetic diversity; present ecological fit vs. climate futures; external silviculture vs. place-based knowledge
summary: Pick tree species that thrive in your local climate, support wildlife, and adapt to future conditions. The right choices now mean forests that last for generations.

title: Choosing What Not to Automate
tension: Efficiency gains vs. human flourishing; instrumental value vs. intrinsic purpose; adaptation vs. identity preservation
summary: Some things shouldn't be automated, even if they could be. Learn how to protect judgment, craft, and meaning while still gaining automation's benefits.

title: Cities Governing Data for Everyone
tension: Data as extractable commodity vs. data as stewarded commons; centralized municipal control vs. resident governance; algorithmic opacity vs. transparent stewardship; vendor lock-in vs. interoperable sovereignty
summary: Cities can treat urban data as a shared resource that residents help govern, ensuring benefits flow back to communities instead of being extracted by outsiders.

title: Cities Learning From Each Other
tension: Jurisdictional autonomy vs. fragmented capacity duplication; isolated innovation vs. systemwide learning velocity
summary: Cities share what works by connecting across neighborhoods and jurisdictions. Peer learning and skill-swapping builds capacity that makes whole regions more resilient.

title: Cities Own Their Digital Tools
tension: Municipal autonomy & digital sovereignty vs. proprietary platform dependency & vendor lock-in
summary: Cities buy and build software they actually control, keeping data local and preventing expensive vendor lock-in. Open code means they can modify tools to fit their needs and share solutions with other cities.

title: Cities Where Every Species Belongs
tension: Sterile urban efficiency (manicured parks, species exclusion, wildlife as pest) vs. Living multispecies interdependence (visible ecology, shared stewardship, animal presence as cultural identity)
summary: Urban spaces designed for humans and wildlife to share power over land, with visible nature, community monitoring, and habitats that adapt to what thrives there.

title: Cities Working Together Across Borders
tension: Municipal autonomy vs. metropolitan equity | Local variation vs. cross-boundary harm
summary: Neighboring cities make binding agreements to solve shared problems—from housing to jobs to services—without losing local control or letting wealthier areas dodge responsibility.

title: Cleaning Up Someone Else's Mess
tension: Historical responsibility vs. present-day stewardship burden; technical remediation vs. community sovereignty over verification and reuse
summary: How communities can hold polluters accountable and turn contaminated land into healthy, shared spaces through systematic restoration and verification.

title: Close the Loop: Urban Water & Nutrients
tension: Linear disposal (water → sewer → treatment → discharge) vs. Cyclical stewardship (water → capture → use → recover → regenerate)
summary: Capture and reuse water and nutrients from homes and businesses instead of losing them. Treat greywater locally and recover valuable phosphorus and nitrogen for farming or gardens.

title: Closing a Business the Right Way
tension: Extractive exit (maximizing financial return to owners) vs. regenerative exit (distributing value justly, preserving capability, protecting mission)
summary: When it's time to wind down, how do you ensure people get their fair share, skills don't disappear, and the work that mattered keeps going?

title: Closing the Loop: Urban Nutrient Cycles
tension: Nutrient extraction (linear waste disposal) vs. nutrient circulation (closed-loop regeneration)
summary: Transform city waste into valuable nutrients by converting organic materials into feed, fertilizer, and soil amendments—keeping resources circulating locally instead of landfilled.

title: Closing the Nutrient Loop
tension: Nutrient extraction vs. nutrient regeneration — the carrying capacity ceiling where harvest must be matched by internal cycling or the system depletes.
summary: Track where nutrients go in your system, find the leaks, and redesign so waste from one part feeds another. Build soil fertility that lasts without needing outside inputs.

title: Closing the Water Loop
tension: Linear extraction (take-treat-discharge) vs. circular regeneration (capture-filter-reuse-infiltrate)
summary: Design water systems that clean and reuse themselves naturally, turning waste into resource while restoring ecosystems and building community resilience.

title: Closing Your Mind When Work Ends
tension: Continuous activation vs. genuine recovery; open loops colonizing consciousness vs. containment and closure
summary: A simple ritual that tells your brain work is done, stops you from replaying the day, and protects your rest time. It's the difference between leaving work and actually leaving work.

title: Communities Buy Their Neighborhood First
tension: Speculative capital (seeking maximum extraction) vs. Community stewardship (seeking stability, belonging, and shared wealth)
summary: When a property goes up for sale, the community gets the chance to buy it before outside investors do. This keeps housing affordable and neighborhoods stable.

title: Communities Buying Land Together
tension: Individual household tenure insecurity vs. collective land stewardship; immediate affordability vs. long-term ownership; scattered negotiating power vs. economies of scale in acquisition
summary: Groups of residents pool money and negotiate as one to buy land they live on, turning temporary agreements into real ownership while spreading both the cost and risk across many people.

title: Communities Decide How Land Gets Used
tension: Land stewardship authority vs. unilateral extraction | Permanence of ecological commitment vs. ownership concentration | Present livelihood vs. intergenerational resilience
summary: A governance structure that gives local communities real power to shape land decisions, approve resource use, and stop harmful changes—with legal teeth and built-in safeguards against power grabs.

title: Communities Decide How Streets Work
tension: Technocratic mobility allocation (speed, routes, space, budgets decided by planners and engineers) vs. Democratic stewardship (residents governing their own movement and public space through participatory assembly)
summary: Residents come together regularly to design and control their own transit and street space, turning transportation from something done to them into something they own and govern together.

title: Communities Decide How to Spend Public Money
tension: Democratic legitimacy vs. fiscal coherence: how to distribute genuine budgetary authority to communities while preventing fragmentation, fungibility capture, and loss of cross-scalar coordination.
summary: Residents gather to directly shape their city's budget, with real legal power and safeguards that protect poorer neighborhoods from being overlooked.

title: Communities Decide How to Spend Public Money
tension: Democratic legitimacy vs. fiscal coherence: how to distribute genuine budgetary authority to communities while preventing fragmentation, fungibility capture, and loss of cross-scalar coordination.
summary: Residents gather to directly shape their city's budget, with real legal power and safeguards that protect poorer neighborhoods from being overlooked.

title: Communities Decide Where Money Goes
tension: Centralized resource control (efficiency, predictability) vs. Distributed voice in allocation (responsiveness, legitimacy, justice)
summary: Let the people affected by a budget actually decide how resources get spent. Make the choices visible, open to challenge, and treat money as a mirror of what a community truly values.

title: Communities Deciding What Their Culture Becomes
tension: Cultural vitality rooted in lived meaning vs. cultural commodification, displacement, and external control
summary: Neighborhoods protect their cultural identity by collectively governing shared spaces—deciding what happens, who belongs, and what stays true to their values over time.

title: Communities Heal the Land They Lost
tension: Historical ecological debt vs. present governance authority — who decides what gets restored, and who benefits from that restoration?
summary: When extraction and dispossession have damaged ecosystems, affected communities lead restoration efforts—reclaiming stewardship, rebuilding health, and making ecological recovery an act of justice.

title: Communities Helping Each Other Stay Strong
tension: Survival interdependence vs. institutional dependency; care as gift vs. care as commodity; local solidarity vs. fragmentation across scale
summary: People pool resources and skills to meet urgent needs—food, housing, care—while building real power together instead of relying on systems that drain from them.

title: Communities Imagining Their Own Futures
tension: Futures-as-imposed (designed by external powers, technocrats, capital) vs. Futures-as-stewarded (collectively imagined, governed, and inhabited by those most affected)
summary: When people shape their own vision of what comes next instead of accepting futures designed by others, they gain real power over their lives and neighborhoods. This means building capacity for collective foresight while honoring different cultures, timelines, and ways of knowing.

title: Communities Keep Their Stories Alive
tension: Cultural erasure through aestheticization and property speculation vs. living memory stewarded by residents as foundation for collective futures
summary: When residents document and govern their own cultural heritage, they build real roots against displacement. Adaptive reuse of meaningful spaces keeps communities grounded through generations.

title: Communities Measuring Their Own Environmental Burden
tension: Hidden cumulative harms vs. visible, governed accountability
summary: Local people map and measure the pollution and hazards affecting their neighborhoods, then gain real power to block harmful projects and hold decision-makers accountable.

title: Communities Monitoring Their Own Land
tension: Scientific rigor vs. community participation — balancing data reliability with distributed knowledge-making and local authority
summary: When people design and run their own ecological monitoring, they learn what the data means, share power over what counts as evidence, and make better decisions about land they care for.

title: Communities Own and Govern Their Land
tension: Administrative Control vs. Resident Stewardship — CLTs risk becoming benevolent landlords (preserving affordability but concentrating decision-making) rather than commons (distributing governance and enforcement to residents).
summary: Residents collectively decide how shared land is used and hold each other accountable through transparent processes. It shifts power from distant managers to the people who live there.

title: Communities Own Their Own Data
tension: Data as extractive asset (held by distant corporations/institutions, generating value that flows away) vs. Data as commons stewardship (held locally, generating value that circulates within community)
summary: Neighborhoods decide who collects their data, who sees it, and what happens next. Power shifts from extraction to stewardship, with communities as trustees.

title: Communities Taking Control of Energy
tension: Individual prosumer atomization vs. collective energy stewardship
summary: Neighbors band together to manage their own power—selling flexibility back to the grid, negotiating fair rates with utilities, and sharing the money equitably. It builds resilient energy systems owned by the people who use them.

title: Communities Taking Water Into Their Own Hands
tension: Centralized utility control & information asymmetry vs. distributed knowledge, accountability, and adaptive commons governance
summary: When people can see how water flows through their city and have a real say in decisions, they care for it differently. This is about building the systems that make that possible.

title: Communities Tell Their Own Stories
tension: Residents as subjects of external narratives vs. residents as authors of their own knowledge and accountability
summary: Neighborhoods run their own media—radio, print, digital—to share what matters locally, hold power accountable, and keep control of their narrative instead of waiting for outside outlets to tell it.

title: Communities That Recover Together
tension: Speed & dignity vs. bureaucracy & conditionality | Local control vs. external aid | Asset protection vs. predatory recovery
summary: Neighborhoods save and manage emergency funds and resources together so families can rebuild quickly after disaster without losing their homes or livelihoods.

title: Communities Watching Nature Together
tension: Real-time adaptive response vs. affordability and local accountability; centralized expertise vs. distributed stewardship knowledge
summary: Local people and sensors spread across a region detect changes in water and soil before they become crises, sharing real data that helps everyone make better decisions about land care.

title: Community Air Watch
tension: Invisible structural pollution (borne by vulnerable neighborhoods) vs. visible community data (that triggers accountability and shifts power)
summary: Empower residents to measure and monitor air quality in their neighborhoods, prioritizing vulnerable communities and using their data to drive environmental action.

title: Community Care for Death & Burial
tension: Catastrophic individual death costs vs. collective ceremonial obligation | Commodified death services vs. dignity-governed ritual | Linear time (development progress) vs. cyclical ancestral presence
summary: Neighbors pool resources to afford funerals and jointly manage burial sites, ensuring everyone receives dignified rites regardless of income.

title: Community-Driven Platform Oversight
tension: Platform utility vs. platform capture: tools designed to amplify distributed voice become extractive intermediaries when governance, fees, and design logic remain opaque and irreversible.
summary: Give residents real power to audit city platforms, verify decisions, and keep them true to their public mission through transparent governance and shared oversight.

title: Community-Led Accessibility Enforcement
tension: Accessibility as post-hoc compliance vs. accessibility as live, distributed governance; expertise extracted from disabled people vs. disabled people as sovereign auditors with enforcement power
summary: Disabled residents lead audits of public spaces and hold cities accountable for accessibility. Communities document barriers and push for real enforcement of access standards.

title: Community-Led Cities: Shared Power Over Land
tension: Participation at scale (depth vs. coverage) vs. Capacity constraints (who decides with limited resources)
summary: Cities where residents and officials jointly decide land use and development. This blends official governance with neighborhood input, giving communities real control over their spaces.

title: Community-Led Dispute Resolution
tension: Accessibility & cultural legitimacy (local adjudication) vs. fairness & appeal (higher authority)
summary: Empower neighborhoods to resolve conflicts through trusted community members and elders, with clear pathways to formal courts when needed.

title: Community-Led Research That Works
tension: Extraction vs. Co-Stewardship: Expert-defined research questions and external ownership of findings vs. community-led problem framing and shared knowledge governance.
summary: Residents and researchers partner as equals to ask important questions, solve local problems together, and build shared knowledge that benefits neighborhoods.

title: Community-Owned Internet Networks
tension: Treating connectivity infrastructure as a privatizable commodity vs. stewarding it as living commons that adapts to community needs and persists across generations.
summary: Cities build affordable, reliable internet by establishing public fiber networks and cooperative broadband systems that serve residents as shared utilities rather than private monopolies.

title: Community Power: Local Energy Cooperatives
tension: Centralized corporate energy infrastructure (concentrating power and profits) vs. distributed community-owned energy commons (distributing ownership, governance, and benefits)
summary: Empower neighborhoods to own and manage renewable energy together, while helping fossil fuel workers transition to new green jobs that keep them rooted in their communities.

title: Community Watchdogs for City Government
tension: Institutional legitimacy erodes when citizens cannot verify municipal decisions, yet top-down auditing neither rebuilds trust nor scales. Decentralized accountability without coordination becomes noise; centralized oversight without citizen participation recreates the capture it seeks to prevent.
summary: Residents form inspection teams to audit municipal spending, investigate misconduct, and strengthen transparency through direct oversight of local government.

title: Connect Ideas Across Different Fields
tension: Siloed expertise (depth without breadth) vs. shallow polymathy (breadth without coherence)
summary: Learn to spot patterns in one field and apply them to another. This breaks down silos and creates breakthroughs that single disciplines can't reach alone.

title: Connected Cities, Independent Neighborhoods
tension: Coherence at scale vs. legitimacy through proximity — how to coordinate across neighborhoods without concentrating power or erasing local voice.
summary: Enable neighborhoods to operate autonomously while seamlessly sharing data and services across city platforms. Multiple governance levels collaborate without forcing everyone into a single system.

title: Connecting Fragmented Habitats
tension: Physical connectivity vs. functional gene flow — habitat corridors can appear intact yet fail to sustain the genetic exchange that populations need to adapt and persist.
summary: Design living corridors that let wildlife move freely across broken landscapes, using genetic signals to measure whether populations can actually survive and adapt.

title: Connecting Habitats for Pollinators
tension: Landscape fragmentation (isolated habitat patches) vs. pollinator movement need (continuous pathways for foraging, migration, genetic exchange)
summary: Create pathways of flowers and nesting spots across fragmented land so pollinators can move, feed, and thrive. It takes coordinated care over time and across property lines.

title: Connecting Today's Choices to Tomorrow's Life
tension: immediate urgency vs. long-term flourishing
summary: How to make decisions now that actually serve your long-term wellbeing. Map what matters across different time scales, so you're not trading your future for today's comfort.

title: Connecting Wildlife Across Broken Landscapes
tension: Generative capacity vs. carrying limits — some patches must produce surplus; others depend on that flow; misalignment converts sources to sinks and collapses the network.
summary: Map which habitat patches are thriving and which are struggling, then link them with corridors so animals can move freely. This keeps populations alive even when individual areas face hardship.

title: Connecting Wildlife Across Broken Landscapes
tension: Generative capacity vs. carrying limits — some patches must produce surplus; others depend on that flow; misalignment converts sources to sinks and collapses the network.
summary: Map which habitat patches are thriving and which are struggling, then link them with corridors so animals can move freely. This keeps populations alive even when individual areas face hardship.

title: Contracts That Grow With You
tension: Contractual certainty vs. systemic adaptability | Protection of buyer interests vs. supplier viability
summary: Move beyond fixed agreements to supplier relationships that adapt as conditions change. Keep trust intact by being transparent about adjustments and sharing burdens fairly.

title: Controlling Overtime Before It Controls You
tension: Worker protection vs. operational flexibility | Cost control vs. fair compensation | Individual agency vs. systemic limits
summary: Set up approval gates that make overtime costs visible and keep them fair. Stewards decide when extra hours happen, balancing what workers need, what the organization can handle, and what the law allows.

title: Controlling What Rot Releases
tension: Anaerobic carbon fate: release as methane (GHG) vs. retain as digestate (fertility) — mediated by oxygen availability, microbial community, and deliberate pathway steering
summary: Manage the invisible chemistry of decomposition to decide whether dead matter becomes greenhouse gas or new soil. The difference lies in oxygen and microbes.

title: Cool Cities That Don't Displace People
tension: Retrofit urgency (climate, health) vs. occupancy continuity and affordability (displacement, exclusion)
summary: Retrofit buildings and neighborhoods to share cooling benefits fairly, using passive design and community care to prevent heat inequality and displacement in mixed-income areas.

title: Cooling Cities With Trees and Surfaces
tension: Thermal equity vs. thermal exposure: some neighborhoods experience large temperature differentials while lacking canopy access; systematic cooling requires both measurement and justice-centered allocation.
summary: Plant trees and use light-colored surfaces strategically to reduce dangerous heat in neighborhoods, especially in places that need it most.

title: Cooperative Platforms for Fairer Cities
tension: Network Effects & Lock-in vs. Democratic Ownership & Portability
summary: Community-owned digital platforms that give users control over their data and enable switching between services, reshaping how urban services are governed.

title: Corridors That Keep Invaders Out
tension: Native dispersal vs. invasive spread — both exploit the same pathways; corridors amplify whichever force gains dominance
summary: Design habitat pathways that let native species move freely while blocking invasive ones. Think of them as living boundaries that adapt as threats change.

title: Counting What a Watershed Gives Us
tension: Invisible ecosystem work vs. visible economic activity — the flows that sustain life go unmeasured while the activities that degrade them command all resources and attention
summary: Measure the water, clean air, and other gifts a watershed provides, value them fairly, and share both the benefits and the work of protecting them among everyone who depends on it.

title: Counting What Really Matters
tension: Hidden externalities (environmental costs treated as free) vs. Visible throughput (all flows—material, energetic, ecological—counted in real time)
summary: Accounting systems that put environmental costs into business decisions, so companies measure true impact instead of just profit and loss.

title: Create Patchwork Habitats for More Life
tension: Homogenization vs. Heterogeneity — the pressure toward simplification and monoculture versus the ecological truth that diversity emerges from fine-scale differentiation
summary: Design small-scale variety in soil, moisture, and light so different species thrive together in the same space. Builds resilience and rich ecosystems without needing vast land.

title: Create Your Own Market
tension: Capture vs. Create — the choice between extracting share from existing competitors or cultivating entirely new ground where competition becomes irrelevant.
summary: Stop fighting for scraps in crowded spaces. Instead, explore the edges where new possibilities emerge and stake out territory no one's competing for yet.

title: Creating Living Edges Between Habitats
tension: Hard edges (fragmentation, microclimatic stress, predation) vs. Soft gradients (diversity, connectivity, resilience)
summary: Soft, gradual boundaries between different habitats support more species and help animals move safely across fragmented land. These transition zones become rich ecosystems in their own right.

title: Creating Pathways for Climate-Shifting Species
tension: Species' evolutionary timescale vs. climate change velocity: adapting in place or moving to new homes; preserving what was vs. enabling what will be.
summary: Design corridors that let animals and plants move as their climate zones shift, keeping populations connected and giving them room to adapt as the world warms.

title: Creating Pathways for Wildlife and Water
tension: Fragmentation vs. connectivity — isolated patches cannot sustain populations; yet open movement invites invasives and disease. Permeability must be selective, not universal.
summary: Find out where animals, plants, and water can move freely across your landscape, and where barriers block them. Design corridors that reconnect fragmented habitats while protecting sensitive areas.

title: Creating Rituals That Last
tension: Continuity vs. Rigidity: How to create durable, meaningful ritual that holds identity and transmits values without calcifying into obligation or excluding those whose lives don't fit the original form.
summary: Design ceremonies that pass down what matters most—values, stories, identity—in ways that can bend with changing times without breaking.

title: Creating Safe Passages for Predators
tension: Predator Movement & Survival vs. Human Settlement & Livestock Protection
summary: Design wildlife corridors that let apex predators roam freely across fragmented landscapes, keeping ecosystems balanced and reducing conflicts between humans and wildlife.

title: Creating Safe Paths for Wild Animals
tension: Habitat fragmentation (isolation, genetic bottleneck, mortality) vs. Connected movement (resilience, adaptation, survival)
summary: Remove obstacles and design safe passages so wildlife can move freely through cities and fragmented landscapes without getting hit or blocked.

title: Creating Symbols That Bind Neighborhoods
tension: Atomization & invisibility vs. collective self-recognition & stewarded identity
summary: Neighbors work together to design and care for the symbols, rituals, and stories that make their place feel like home—and help people stay connected across differences.

title: Creating Walkable, Connected Neighborhoods
tension: Enclosure (mega-blocks, sealed boundaries, institutional monoliths) vs. Permeability (fine-grain networks, permeable edges, interior activation)
summary: Design cities with permeable blocks and connected street networks that encourage walking and movement between neighborhoods, while thoughtfully managing edges and boundaries.

title: Creating Winter Shelters for City Wildlife
tension: Urban thermal erasure (heated surfaces, cleared litter, sealed cavities) vs. creation of differentiated microrefugia that enable overwintering survival and year-round thermal diversity.
summary: Design hidden warm spots across urban spaces—in rocks, soil, and cavities—where cold-blooded animals and hibernating creatures can survive harsh winters safely.

title: Creating Work That Fully Absorbs You
tension: Shallow fragmentation vs. deep absorption | Burnout through flow-dependency vs. stagnation through insufficient challenge
summary: Design the conditions where challenge matches skill so people get lost in meaningful work. Balance difficulty, environment, and recovery to sustain that deep engagement.

title: Creative Spaces Where Artists Thrive Together
tension: Artist survival & cultural vitality vs. market displacement & institutional gatekeeping
summary: Artists share affordable housing, studios, and resources while building financial security through mutual support and collaborative learning communities.

title: Decide Which Species and Habitats Matter Most
tension: Preserving all life vs. stewarding finite resources; precaution vs. pragmatism; universal equity vs. strategic focus
summary: Choose which endangered ecosystems and animals to protect first using systematic ranking methods. Learn assessment frameworks that help conservation teams allocate limited resources where they'll have the biggest impact.

title: Deciding by What Actually Matters
tension: Abstract values vs. concrete decisions; coherence vs. paralysis; authentic priorities vs. inherited conditioning
summary: Get clear on your core values, rank them, then use them to make decisions. It keeps you aligned with what you believe instead of just what's easy.

title: Deciding What to Do With Profits
tension: Extraction (maximizing near-term distribution) vs. Regeneration (reinvesting for long-term vitality)
summary: How to share earnings with stakeholders while keeping enough to grow, staying honest about what your business can actually sustain.

title: Deciding What to Fix or Discard
tension: Economic recovery (rework, regrade, salvage) vs. Quality assurance (scrap, containment, risk mitigation)
summary: Set up clear rules for when damaged materials get repaired versus thrown away, with transparent approval processes and complete tracking so you learn from each decision.

title: Deciding What's Worth Buying
tension: Empowering local stewards to move resources quickly vs. preserving systemic oversight so capital allocations align with shared carrying capacity and just distribution across the whole.
summary: Groups set clear spending limits and approval chains so big purchases get the right level of review. This keeps money flowing toward what matters most and what the organization can actually sustain.

title: Deciding When to Pivot or Close
tension: Acting with urgency when signals emerge vs. Acting with wisdom, grounded in values and collective understanding
summary: Make tough decisions about your organization's future before crisis forces your hand. Clear frameworks, honest signals, and aligned stakeholders help you change course or close gracefully—without burning relationships or losing yourself.

title: Deciding Which Features Actually Matter
tension: Continuous feature creation vs. finite development capacity and cognitive load; decoupling deployment from activation vs. inventory accumulation and technical debt.
summary: Listen to how people use your product, then deliberately choose what to build, change, or retire. Let real adoption data guide what stays.

title: Defending Urban Commons from Collapse
tension: Stewardship Capacity & Autonomy vs. Structural Decay Pressures (accumulation, commodification, debt, external flows, scale mismatch, power asymmetry)
summary: Urban commons survive only when communities actively protect them from being seized, sold off, or controlled by outside interests. Without constant defense of who decides, what counts as boundary, and staying appropriately sized, commons fail.

title: Democracy Through Nested Communities
tension: Representation at scale (broad legitimacy) vs. depth of voice (marginalized communities heard, not absorbed)
summary: Build trust and representation by organizing governance through layers of smaller groups—neighborhoods elect representatives to city level, creating direct voice at every scale while honoring diverse identities.

title: Design Gardens That Feed Pollinators
tension: Pollinator scarcity & monofloral starvation vs. ecological restoration through living floral diversity
summary: Plant flowers strategically to match what local bees, butterflies, and other pollinators need year-round. The right mix keeps them thriving and your crops pollinated.

title: Design Interfaces People Trust
tension: Competing for attention (dark patterns, cognitive overload, manipulation) vs. serving comprehension and agency (legibility, honest feedback, user-centered stewardship)
summary: Build clear, responsive interfaces where every button and form tells users what to do next. Good design reduces confusion and helps people get things done.

title: Design Life as a Cycle of Renewal
tension: Extraction vs. Regeneration — the choice between taking more than you return (leading to depletion and collapse) versus designing every cycle to restore what it consumes
summary: Build systems where waste becomes food, giving and receiving balance each other, and keeping things healthy is the main job—not just fixing emergencies.

title: Design Plazas Where People Want to Stay
tension: Designed emptiness vs. emergent vitality; abstract aesthetics vs. embodied usability; designer intent vs. community stewardship
summary: Create public squares with varied ground textures, subtle level changes, and welcoming edges that naturally draw people together and let communities shape the space through everyday use.

title: Design That Grows With You
tension: Standardization vs. Localization — How to create coherent, replicable value while honoring context, agency, and adaptive capacity.
summary: Build systems from pieces that fit together in different ways, so communities can adapt them to what they actually need instead of replacing everything from scratch.

title: Design Your Home as a Living System
tension: The home as refuge vs. the home as production machine; restoration vs. function; shared territory vs. individual sanctuary.
summary: Create physical and temporal boundaries in your home that restore focus, enable deep work, and build resilience. Intentional spaces—from biophilic zones to sacred retreats—turn your domestic threshold into a system that sustains you.

title: Design Your Life Around Natural Rhythms
tension: Linear perpetual-growth expectations vs. cyclical reality of human energy, attention, and seasons
summary: Treat your life like a living system with seasons—busy times and rest times. Plan ahead for what's coming, match your commitments to your actual energy, and make choices you can reverse when seasons change.

title: Design Your Life Like a Commons
tension: Intrinsic worth vs. conditional achievement | Finite resources vs. infinite demands | Self-care vs. contribution to others
summary: Your time and energy are shared resources. Align them with what matters, build others up, and rest intentionally—so your life sustains itself and the people who depend on you.

title: Design Your Own Growth
tension: Personal growth as isolated self-improvement vs. personal development as a commons act of stewardship
summary: Shape who you're becoming through reflection, practice, and learning with others. Treat your development like a living system that improves through cycles of action, feedback, and shared insight.

title: Design Your Role with Purpose
tension: Role coherence (identity, purpose, boundaries) vs. Role multiplicity (competing demands, identity bleed, transition friction)
summary: Shape your work so it feels coherent and meaningful—clarifying what you do, how much freedom you have, and how it fits who you are. This keeps your role from pulling you in conflicting directions.

title: Design Your Sleep Like a Living System
tension: Sleep as fixed personal habit vs. sleep as a designed, shared, adaptive system requiring continuous stewardship
summary: Sleep is foundational to everything else. Treat it as an experiment you actively shape—aligned with your rhythms, negotiated with housemates, and adjusted as your body changes.

title: Designing Cities for Young People
tension: Adult-designed cities that erase children's futures vs. youth-led stewardship that creates thriving, convivial neighborhoods for all generations
summary: Engage young people in creating safer, more welcoming neighborhoods where they belong. Involve them in planning spaces and preventing displacement through participatory design.

title: Designing Gradual Transitions Between Street and Home
tension: Density without anonymity: How to enable close inhabitation while preserving the ability to regulate exposure and maintain coherent community identity across nested scales.
summary: Create welcoming passages and courtyards that ease people from the busy street into private spaces, using layered thresholds instead of walls. This gives neighborhoods character and makes people feel genuinely invited rather than blocked.

title: Designing Living Buffers for Healthy Streams
tension: Buffer adequacy vs. land use pressure — how wide, how structured, how monitored to persist as living systems rather than static reserves?
summary: Plant strategic strips of vegetation along waterways to filter pollution, prevent erosion, and keep water cool. Size and plant them to match what your specific stream needs.

title: Designing Partnerships That Last
tension: Implicit assumptions & hidden power dynamics vs. Explicit agreements & transparent governance
summary: Build relationships that stay healthy and fair by being clear about power, boundaries, and what you're all working toward together.

title: Designing Real Recovery
tension: Premature return to function vs. insufficient restoration; generic protocols vs. nervous-system-calibrated practices
summary: Recovery isn't downtime—it's skilled work that rebuilds capacity and prevents burnout. Design your restoration phases as carefully as you design your main work.

title: Designing Sleep as Shared Infrastructure
tension: Sleep as luxury vs. sleep as non-negotiable commons infrastructure; individual optimization vs. systemic cultural transformation
summary: Sleep is a commons we neglect at our peril. When we design for better sleep—spaces, rhythms, rituals—we regenerate the cognitive and emotional capacity we need to show up for each other and do good work together.

title: Designing Spaces Where Humans and Wildlife Thrive
tension: Human settlement expansion & resource use vs. wildlife habitat integrity & coexistence viability
summary: Create buffer zones and gradual transitions between human communities and wild areas that prevent conflict, protect ecosystems, and adapt as both populations change.

title: Designing Street Faces That Engage
tension: Distinctive character vs. coherent identity | Individual expression vs. shared legibility
summary: Create lively, inviting streetscapes through rhythmic facades, transparent ground floors, and thoughtful building edges that draw people in and activate the public realm.

title: Diaspora Money and Trust Networks
tension: Individual survival (remittance consumption) vs. Collective flourishing (homeland enterprise investment); Formal banking (regulated, extractive) vs. Informal networks (trusted, adaptive); Brain drain (loss) vs. Knowledge return (contribution)
summary: How families separated across borders build businesses and send money home through relationships instead of banks. A way to move resources that strengthens both communities.

title: Digital Access Through Trusted Local Places
tension: Universal digital participation vs. systemic exclusion through infrastructure, literacy, and institutional gatekeeping
summary: Communities control digital access through institutions they already trust, with learning programs that build both skills and collective power to make decisions together.

title: Direct Food From Farms to Tables
tension: Margin extraction by intermediaries vs. fair value distribution across the food network
summary: Cut out the middleman and connect farmers directly with eaters through transparent cooperatives that pay producers fairly and keep prices honest.

title: Directing Money Where It Matters
tension: Capital as constraint vs. capital as enabler — between preserving runway and investing in growth; between centralized discipline and distributed agency; between financial returns and systemic impact.
summary: Make capital decisions through clear rules and nested layers of governance. Track what works, stay transparent, and keep enough reserves so the organization stays resilient while funding what matters most.

title: Disabled People Building Accessible Cities
tension: Individual accommodation burden vs. collective accessibility stewardship
summary: Disabled people lead the design and governance of accessibility as shared infrastructure, creating jobs, homes, and support networks that strengthen their economic power and community resilience.

title: Disabled People Design the City
tension: Accessibility-as-afterthought (retrofitted compliance) vs. Accessibility-as-foundational (embedded in all design decisions from inception)
summary: Disabled people have real power over urban design and services—not just input, but veto authority. Accessibility is built in from the start, not added later.

title: Disabled People Leading the Way
tension: Accessibility as checkbox compliance vs. accessibility as alive, evolving practice; Disabled people as passive subjects vs. disabled people as architects of their own belonging.
summary: Making spaces, systems, and decisions genuinely accessible by putting disabled people in charge. Not a checklist—a constant practice of finding barriers and fixing them together.

title: Disagreement as a Health Signal
tension: Unity (false consensus that masks real problems) vs. Fission (conflict that ruptures relationships and collaboration)
summary: Conflict tells you something important about your system. Build structures that let people disagree openly, stay connected, and actually learn from opposing views.

title: Doing Business Across Borders Safely
tension: Regulatory containment (preventing harm, enforcing sovereignty) vs. Economic flow (enabling licit trade, sustaining livelihood across borders)
summary: Navigate the rules that govern what you can trade, with whom, and where—without losing sight of legitimate business that needs to keep moving.

title: Don't Depend on One Customer
tension: Efficiency through focus vs. resilience through diversity
summary: Spread revenue across multiple customers so losing one doesn't sink your business. Track how concentrated your income is and actively work to diversify.

title: Don't Put All Your Life in One Basket
tension: Concentration (single point of failure, catastrophic fragility) vs. Diversification (resilience, adaptive capacity, distributed value creation)
summary: Build a varied life across work, relationships, skills, and meaning so that when one part struggles, the rest keeps you standing.

title: Drawing Lines Around What We Use
tension: Growth logic vs. regenerative stewardship; infinite extraction vs. living thresholds; hoarding vs. equitable distribution
summary: Communities decide how much is enough, then build systems to stay within those limits while sharing what's left over. It's stewardship with real boundaries.

title: Drawing Lines Before Nature Breaks
tension: Prevention (precautionary, adaptive, distributed) vs. Remediation (reactive, concentrated, retrospective)
summary: Make ecological damage visible and measurable by tracking what ecosystems can handle, so we can govern based on nature's limits, not just profit.

title: Drawing Lines That Hold
tension: Boundarylessness (depletion, dissolution, exploitation) vs. Rigid Boundaries (isolation, exclusion, brittleness)
summary: Boundaries aren't walls—they're living edges that protect what matters and let communities thrive. When people practice clear, renegotiable boundaries as stewardship, commons stay healthy and sustainable.

title: Dress Like You Mean It
tension: Conformity to external beauty/fashion standards vs. authentic embodied self-expression rooted in values, sensory comfort, and accessibility
summary: Use clothing as a daily practice that reflects your values, expresses who you are, and treats your body with real care. Turn getting dressed into something intentional.

title: Dust and Air Quality from the Ground Up
tension: Degraded land surfaces (bare soil, exposed carbon, sparse vegetation) release particulates and aerosols that alter atmospheric composition and radiative balance vs. stewarded land surfaces (vegetated, stabilized, living) that suppress emissions and regenerate air quality.
summary: How soil, plants, and land management shape the air we breathe and the climate around us. Tracking dust and pollution helps us see the connection between what happens on land and what happens in the sky.

title: Earning Land Rights Through Use
tension: Tenure security (individual need for protection) vs. Collective stewardship (community's need to prevent alienation and preserve commons)
summary: A system where people gain stronger rights to land by living on it, using it well, and being part of the community—letting newcomers belong while preventing speculation and protecting shared stewardship.

title: Earning Real Authority Through Trust
tension: Position vs. Presence | External Permission vs. Inner Knowing | Self-Interest vs. Service
summary: True influence comes from being reliable and consistent, not from your title. When your judgment matches your actions and you genuinely serve others, people follow you naturally.

title: Earning Trust Before Full Membership
tension: Rapid integration (risk of misalignment) vs. cautious gatekeeping (risk of exclusion and slow adaptation)
summary: New members go through a structured trial period where they demonstrate commitment before gaining full access and decision-making power. Clear checkpoints and transparent standards make the process fair for everyone.

title: Earning Trust Through Real Accountability
tension: Formal compliance vs. genuine community trust; one-time agreement vs. adaptive stewardship
summary: A commons stays legitimate by making promises to its community and keeping them visibly—through honest tracking, real responses to complaints, and genuine two-way conversation.

title: Earning Trust Through Real Listening
tension: Expert authority vs. community sovereignty; Visibility vs. erasure; Technical solution vs. relational foundation
summary: Build legitimate authority by genuinely hearing community voices, being transparent about what changes and what doesn't, and respecting the power structures already at work.

title: Eat With Your Body's Rhythms
tension: Industrial standardization (uniform meals, year-round availability, speed-eating) vs. ecological attunement (seasonal cycles, circadian alignment, digestion quality)
summary: Align your eating patterns with your body's natural cycles and the seasons to improve digestion and energy. Pay attention to when and how you eat, not just what.

title: Eating Safely With Food Allergies
tension: Safety (avoiding harm) vs. Belonging (sharing meals without fear or exclusion)
summary: Learn what your body can and can't handle, stay safe around food, and still enjoy meals with others without anxiety or isolation.

title: Eating Together as Governance
tension: Individual autonomy & nourishment vs. collective ritual & belonging
summary: Shared meals build trust and repair conflict. When you design who eats together, how decisions get made, and what values each meal holds, you create a repeatable ritual that sustains belonging and distributes work fairly.

title: Eating Together, Building Trust
tension: Charity (one-way, stigmatizing, recipient-passive) vs. Commons (reciprocal, dignified, participant-active)
summary: Create shared meals in public spaces where people contribute what they can and decide together how food gets distributed—turning eating into a ritual that rebuilds both nourishment and community across different backgrounds.

title: Eating Your Way Back Home
tension: Cultural erasure vs. embodied continuity — the pressure to assimilate foodways in tension with the imperative to keep ancestral knowledge alive in hands, bodies, and tables.
summary: Food carries your ancestors' knowledge and identity. By cooking, fermenting, and eating together, you recover lost skills, strengthen cultural bonds, and reclaim what colonization tried to erase.

title: Economics That Actually Works
tension: Extractive growth vs. regenerative stewardship
summary: Economies thrive when they align profits with regeneration, share surplus fairly, and respect planetary limits instead of chasing endless growth.

title: Elders as Decision Makers
tension: Knowledge decay & institutional amnesia vs. Elder marginalization & age segregation
summary: Give elders real power in governance and pay them to share what they know. Their experience becomes an institution's memory and guide.

title: Elders Teaching Skills for Pay
tension: Knowledge loss through generational turnover vs. dignified, reciprocal intergenerational transmission
summary: Experienced people earn money by teaching younger people their skills through apprenticeships. It keeps knowledge alive, creates jobs, and builds real relationships across generations.

title: Ending Products Without Breaking Trust
tension: Organizational need to discontinue offerings vs. custodial responsibility to customers who depend on them
summary: When you retire a product or service, how you do it matters as much as the decision itself. A thoughtful transition protects your relationships and helps everyone move forward.

title: Enough is Enough
tension: Scarcity-driven hoarding & consumption vs. abundance-oriented generosity & sufficiency
summary: Practice restraint and celebration together to feel abundant, heal stress, and care for the next generation.

title: Ensuring Fair Representation and Stability
tension: Procedural legitimacy (we follow rules) vs. Substantive justice (our rules produce fair outcomes for all)
summary: Track who benefits from city programs and policies. Hold leaders accountable for racial equity, prevent displacement, and guarantee housing security for all residents.

title: Everyone Gets a Real Say
tension: Efficiency vs. Legitimacy: Fast decisions made by few vs. slow decisions made by all; centralized control vs. diffuse accountability.
summary: Design meetings so all members can genuinely participate and influence decisions, not just attend. When you structure voice into the system itself, you build trust and better outcomes.

title: Everyone Gets Around
tension: Universal access vs. one-size-fits-all design; mobility as individual commodity vs. mobility as collective right; technocratic retrofit vs. participatory stewardship
summary: Design transport systems where all bodies can move with dignity. Co-design with disabled and marginalized communities, embed accessibility into infrastructure, and let communities control what barriers get removed.

title: Everyone's Knowledge Counts in Decisions
tension: Expert authority (concentrated, credentialed, abstracting) vs. Distributed epistemic legitimacy (lived experience, tacit knowledge, vernacular voice)
summary: How to make room for lived experience and different ways of knowing—not just credentialed experts—when communities make decisions together.

title: Evolving Products With Your Customers
tension: Predetermined product roadmaps vs. adaptive responsiveness to actual user needs and system limits
summary: Build products that grow and change with what people actually need, treating your whole lineup as a living system instead of a fixed list.

title: Factories That Learn and Adapt
tension: Centralized, linear extraction (design → produce → dispose) vs. Distributed, cyclical stewardship (sense → adapt → regenerate)
summary: Build manufacturing systems where workers, machines, and materials work together intelligently—sharing information, making decisions locally, and getting smarter over time instead of just following orders.

title: Fair Access to Digital Services for All
tension: Digital convenience vs. digital exclusion; vendor lock-in vs. resident sovereignty; municipal control vs. community stewardship
summary: Ensure everyone can use digital services equally, whether online or offline, keep their data portable, and access support whenever they need it—without being left behind.

title: Fair Access to Urban Land
tension: Equity & Access vs. Tenure Security & Formality
summary: Establish transparent systems and fair processes for who gets urban land, balancing customary practices with formal records to ensure equitable access for all residents.

title: Fair Fares for Everyone
tension: Farebox recovery (pricing for revenue) vs. Access as right (pricing for equity)
summary: Make public transit affordable for all income levels through sliding-scale pricing, smart subsidies, and revenue-sharing across transportation modes.

title: Fair Feedback That Actually Evolves
tension: Consistency vs. Responsiveness — the need for fair, comparable assessment across a distributed organization versus the requirement that feedback remain timely, contextual, and alive to real work conditions.
summary: Create honest, ongoing conversations about how people are doing—with transparent standards and distributed decision-making—so feedback stays useful instead of becoming a box-ticking exercise.

title: Fair Fix: Service Guarantees and Quick Redress
tension: Service as bureaucratic discretion vs. Service as a covenant: Who holds power when the system fails—the institution, or those harmed by its failure?
summary: When city services fail, residents get automatic compensation and direct access to an ombudsman who can escalate issues. Clear delivery standards ensure accountability.

title: Fair Hiring That Actually Works
tension: Consistency vs. Humanity — standardized evaluation can become dehumanizing; unstructured judgment preserves dignity but breeds opacity and inequity.
summary: Create shared standards for evaluating candidates so your hiring reflects your values, not hidden bias. Train interviewers, calibrate assessments, document decisions.

title: Fair Housing Across City Borders
tension: Municipal autonomy vs. metropolitan justice
summary: Coordinate housing access between cities to ensure equitable settlement opportunities and prevent displacement through transparent, algorithmic allocation.

title: Fair Pay for Creators
tension: Cultural authenticity & localized meaning vs. scaled market reach & economic viability
summary: Design systems that get money to artists fairly, protect cultural integrity, and sustain the communities where creative work thrives.

title: Fair Pay That Reflects Values
tension: Fair reciprocity vs. Market pressure | Transparency vs. Privacy | Individual negotiation vs. Systemic equity
summary: Set wages together based on what people contribute and need, not just market forces. Make the numbers transparent and rooted in what your community actually believes is fair.

title: Fair Prices Across Different Regions
tension: Local autonomy & market responsiveness vs. system coherence & fair access
summary: How to set different prices in different places without losing trust. Document why prices vary, approve changes fairly, and check that everyone gets a good deal.

title: Fair Pricing That Works for Everyone
tension: Information asymmetry & extraction vs. Transparency & reciprocal burden-sharing
summary: Stop hiding real costs in supply chains. Show what things actually cost, share the burden fairly, and adjust prices as conditions change—turning buying into honest partnership instead of squeezing suppliers.

title: Fair Resilience When Climate Hits Hardest
tension: Imposed climate stress (from distant emitters) vs. local adaptive capacity and self-determination
summary: Communities facing the worst climate impacts design their own solutions that share the burden fairly, pool resources together, and keep decisions local. This is adaptation that centers justice.

title: Fair Rest and Return to Work
tension: Individual need for rest and life continuity vs. collective need for operational reliability and fairness
summary: How organizations handle time off so people can recharge while keeping operations steady. Fair accrual, clear rules, and dignified comeback matter for everyone.

title: Fair Ways to Share Costs
tension: Hiding distributed costs (opacity, buck-passing, distorted incentives) vs. Making costs visible and fairly attributed (transparency, reciprocity, true stewardship)
summary: Divide shared expenses so everyone sees what they're paying for and why. Builds trust and makes sure costs land fairly on those who benefit most.

title: Family Land, Shared Responsibility
tension: Individual security vs. collective continuity; formalization vs. customary fluidity; women's protection vs. patrilineal control
summary: Land passed down through family lines with built-in safeguards: ceremonies mark transitions, obligations keep everyone accountable, and rules protect women and widows from losing their stake.

title: Farmers Growing and Governing Seeds
tension: Seed as commodity vs. seed as commons. Corporate control and genetic monopoly vs. farmer autonomy and agrobiodiversity.
summary: Communities take control of seed breeding, sharing, and decision-making instead of depending on corporations. It's about keeping seeds as a shared resource and making sure farmers benefit from the work they do.

title: Farming Knowledge That Travels Through Time
tension: Knowledge preservation vs. adaptive evolution—holding what works while remaining responsive to changing conditions
summary: Bring farmers, researchers, and land stewards together to document, test, and share what works—creating living knowledge that adapts, stays rooted in place, and lasts for generations.

title: Farming Mussels to Clean Water
tension: Benthic abundance vs. system carrying capacity — more filter-feeders improve water clarity until they exceed plankton production and collapse.
summary: Grow bivalve populations that naturally filter and stabilize water ecosystems. Match stocking to what the local environment can support, then monitor to keep things in balance.

title: Feed Your Inner Ecosystem
tension: Generic dietary prescription vs. personalized, adaptive nutritional stewardship
summary: Learn what your unique body needs to thrive by understanding your microbiome. Match your eating to your personal biology, not generic advice.

title: Feed Your Soil, Feed Your Crops
tension: Nutrient supply (what soil biology releases when) vs. nutrient demand (what crops need when)
summary: Learn how nutrients cycle through soil and compost to match what your plants actually need and when they need it most.

title: Feedback That Builds People Up
tension: Accountability (proving worth through metrics) vs. Development (building capacity through trust and visibility)
summary: Replace annual judgments with ongoing conversations that help people grow, let teams set their own standards, and treat everyone with respect through every transition.

title: Feeding Pollinators Through Every Season
tension: Temporal mismatch (pollinators present but flowers absent; flowers blooming but pollinators dormant) vs. Phenological synchrony (flowers and pollinators aligned across the full cycle)
summary: Design gardens and farms so flowers bloom continuously year-round, matching when pollinators need food. This keeps them healthy and ensures they stick around to pollinate your crops.

title: Feel Deeply Without Getting Lost
tension: Empathic connection vs. empathic overwhelm; feeling with others vs. feeling *for* them; translating understanding into appropriate action vs. self-sacrificial enabling.
summary: Develop real empathy that stays accurate and boundaried. Feel what others feel, but stay clear about what's yours and what's theirs—so you can actually help.

title: Festivals That Pay Back Communities
tension: Economic vitality vs. cultural authenticity & community displacement
summary: A festival can generate genuine economic benefit for the people and culture it celebrates—when it's built on fair pay, transparent money flows, and shared decision-making.

title: Finding a Pace That Works Together
tension: Imposed pace (speed optimized for systems) vs. Sustainable pace (speed optimized for people and relationships)
summary: Talk openly about how fast you're moving and adjust together. When everyone's rhythm is visible and negotiable, the work feels sustainable and less chaotic.

title: Finding and Mapping Your Soil Carbon
tension: Invisible carbon distribution vs. visible management decisions; point-in-time measurement vs. trajectory of change
summary: Discover where carbon is stored in your soil at different depths and locations. This knowledge helps you build better land stewardship and lasting climate resilience.

title: Finding and Protecting Nature's Irreplaceable Places
tension: Invisible Uniqueness vs. Visible Threat — endemic species and hotspots exist undetected until mapped, yet mapping without participatory governance and adaptive protection creates extractive conservation.
summary: Map where rare species cluster and how they're changing, so communities can work together to keep these living treasures safe.

title: Finding and Protecting Tiny Climate Refuges
tension: Landscape-scale climate planning vs. the microclimatic specificity where species actually survive
summary: Identify and safeguard the small pockets where plants and animals survive extreme conditions. These hidden sanctuaries are crucial stepping stones for nature to adapt to climate change.

title: Finding Awe in Everyday Life
tension: Instrumental doing vs. contemplative being; ego-bounded self-interest vs. recognition of cosmic insignificance and interconnection
summary: Build a regular practice of experiencing awe—that feeling of wonder and connection to something larger than yourself—to find deeper meaning and guide your choices.

title: Finding Common Ground Across Differences
tension: Winner-take-all position-staking vs. joint problem-ownership; Fixed problem definition vs. collectively-shaped framing
summary: Turn conflict into collaboration by bringing people together to talk openly, understand what matters to each side, and build agreements everyone can live with.

title: Finding Purpose Within Your Work
tension: Vocation vs. Livelihood — the pull between intrinsic calling and instrumental necessity, between designing work and accepting constraints.
summary: How to know what matters to you in a job, claim agency even in roles you didn't design, and regularly check that you're not losing yourself in the process.

title: Finding What Really Matters
tension: Living as if you have infinite time vs. Living consciously within finite time
summary: Face what's finite about life to figure out what you actually value, then build daily habits that match those values.

title: Finding Where Change Actually Happens
tension: Ubiquitous opportunity to intervene vs. the scarcity of true leverage points; surface-level fixes vs. foundational paradigm shifts
summary: Learn to spot the few places in a system where your effort creates real change, and skip the spots that drain energy. Map the flows of power and resources, then act where it matters most.

title: Finding Your Next Move
tension: Predictable advancement vs. adaptive resilience
summary: Map out where your skills matter most and spot opportunities at the edges of what you know. Position yourself to grow in ways that feel right for you.

title: Finding Your People the Right Way
tension: Pull (earned discovery through shared value) vs. Push (paid extraction masquerading as connection)
summary: Reach potential members through trusted channels and voices that work for them, not just you. Build genuine discovery where value flows both directions.

title: Finding Your Place in Nature
tension: Fixed self vs. embedded self | Generic positioning vs. ecological niche | Adaptation vs. authenticity
summary: Understand who you are within living systems and where you fit. Position yourself distinctly, then actively shape the conditions where you and your ecosystem can thrive together.

title: Finding Your Place in Nature's Balance
tension: Power and responsibility vs. denial and false innocence
summary: Understand whether you're predator, prey, or partner in your ecosystem, then steward that role honestly instead of dominating or pretending it doesn't exist.

title: Finding Your Rhythm Again
tension: Chaotic drift vs. premature return to old patterns
summary: After crisis or loss breaks your daily patterns, rebuild them gradually and intentionally. Small rituals and phases help you recover coherence and move forward.

title: Finding Your Voice Online
tension: Derivative learning vs. authentic originality; Private integrity vs. public expression; Individual voice vs. systemic amplification
summary: Develop a genuine, recognizable way of expressing yourself across different platforms. Stay consistent while staying true to who you are, even as you grow and change.

title: Finding Your Way Through Complicity
tension: Acknowledging real complicity vs. maintaining motivation and moral agency
summary: Understand where you're tangled in harmful systems without getting stuck. Map what you can actually change versus what you're caught in, so you can act with clear eyes and real power.

title: Fire as Indigenous Land Medicine
tension: Fire suppression (external control, monoculture, catastrophic risk, knowledge loss) vs. Fire stewardship (distributed authority, cultural practice, ecosystem regeneration, living knowledge)
summary: Indigenous communities use controlled burning to restore healthy ecosystems and pass down generations of land knowledge—now backed by law and formal recognition.

title: Fishing Communities Managing Their Own Waters
tension: Local livelihood security vs. ecosystem regeneration capacity across fragmented jurisdictions
summary: Coastal communities govern shared fisheries together, balancing livelihoods with fish recovery. Multiple groups coordinate across borders through agreements that respect both people and ecosystems.

title: Fixing Problems Where Work Happens
tension: Degradation (entropy, drift toward defect) vs. Continuous Renewal (learning, adaptation, prevention)
summary: Spot issues the moment they appear and fix them together as part of your everyday work. Make problems visible to everyone, involve the whole team in getting better, and build improvement into how you work each day.

title: Follow the Facts Back to Source
tension: Conviction vs. Humility — the need to act decisively while remaining open to being wrong
summary: Stop taking claims at face value. Learn to trace ideas back to where they started, actively look for evidence that proves you wrong, and show your work. It's how you move from just believing things to actually knowing them.

title: Following Water Pollution to Its Source
tension: Hidden externalities vs. visible responsibility — between diffuse pollution that spreads unseen and the clarity required for collective stewardship.
summary: Track where water gets polluted, how much, and where it goes. Visibility creates accountability and points the way to real solutions upstream.

title: Food as Community Health Infrastructure
tension: Food as commodity (extracted, optimized, inequitable) vs. Food as commons (cultivated, shared, just, resilient)
summary: Communities govern their food systems together—growing, sharing, and eating as core health work. When neighbors decide what gets grown and who gets fed, food security becomes a shared commitment.

title: Food, Housing, and Work as One System
tension: Food as market commodity (externalized costs, precarious labor, access by ability-to-pay) vs. food as shared commonwealth (integrated stewardship, living wages, universal nutrition security)
summary: A cooperative where neighbors grow food together, live together, and share the profits—making sure everyone eats well, earns fairly, and has a real say in how things run.

title: Food That Feeds Your Values
tension: Abundance vs. Access: Food is simultaneously abundant and unequally distributed; cheap and ethically costly; nourishing and wasteful. Navigate this paradox without paralysis.
summary: Source food transparently, prepare it skillfully, and spend money in ways that match what you believe in. The result: nourishment that's fair, regenerative, and works within real budgets.

title: Forests That Hold Water
tension: Immediate water extraction vs. long-term hydrological integrity; forest cover vs. water yield; flood peaks vs. dry-season flows
summary: Healthy forests work like giant sponges, capturing rain and releasing it slowly to sustain streams, ecosystems, and communities through dry seasons.

title: Forgiving Debt Together
tension: Debt as perpetual obligation vs. Debt as erasable through collective witness and renewal
summary: Communities periodically erase debts collectively, breaking cycles that trap people and rebuilding trust through fresh starts.

title: From Informal to Formal Waste Work
tension: Invisible informal labour vs. visible cooperative ownership | Waste as disposal cost vs. waste as stewarded resource | Worker exploitation vs. worker governance
summary: Support waste workers in forming cooperatives and gaining legal recognition, transforming precarious livelihoods into stable, dignified work with ownership and fair income.

title: From Informal to Secure Housing
tension: Tenure security vs. displacement risk; formalization as protection vs. formalization as dispossession
summary: Help residents in informal settlements gain legal recognition and stable tenure through formalization pathways that balance paperwork with practical protection against displacement and eviction.

title: From Reactive to Responsive
tension: Reactivity (automatic response to stimulus) vs. Responsiveness (choice grounded in clear seeing)
summary: Build a steadier mind through practice, moving from automatic reactions to thoughtful responses. This opens space for wiser choices in daily life.

title: From Strangers to Neighbors
tension: Anonymity & isolation vs. premature intimacy demands; stranger-danger hypervigilance vs. genuine openness; weak-tie scarcity vs. loneliness infrastructure gap.
summary: Turn urban anonymity into real connection through welcoming rituals, regular casual encounters, and spaces where people naturally meet. Trust grows when newcomers belong from day one.

title: From Street Vendors to Legitimate Businesses
tension: Legal protection vs. cultural autonomy; individual survival vs. collective resilience; formalization pathways vs. displacement risk
summary: Street food vendors organize together to gain legal status and market access while staying true to their culture and independence. A path that respects their work instead of shutting it down.

title: Funding Accessible Cities for Everyone
tension: Accessibility as episodic compliance project (one-time, reversible, cost-shifted to disabled residents) vs. Accessibility as permanent commons infrastructure (perpetual, irreversible, collectively stewarded, publicly financed)
summary: Establish permanent financing for accessibility upgrades in cities while ensuring costs don't fall on disabled people. Make inclusive infrastructure a shared responsibility, not an afterthought.

title: Funding Without Losing Control
tension: Founder autonomy & mission continuity vs. capital acquisition & investor return demands
summary: Navigate investment rounds while protecting your mission and autonomy. Learn how to use equity strategically, manage dilution, and find investors who share your values.

title: Getting Approval Before You Commit
tension: Authority distribution vs. commitment clarity — how to disperse decision-making while ensuring every commitment is binding, auditable, and adaptive
summary: Set up clear checkpoints so offers and requests get the right approvals, everyone knows who decided what, and you can track the whole thing from start to finish.

title: Getting Around Together
tension: Private mobility capture vs. shared mobility stewardship | Individual vehicle ownership vs. collective access | Profit extraction vs. reinvestment in equity
summary: Communities govern shared mobility—transit, bikes, scooters, walking—as commons instead of letting private companies control them. The result: less traffic, fairer access, fewer cars needed.

title: Getting Better at Handling Your Emotions
tension: Emotional reactivity (amygdala hijack, flooding, escalation) vs. Emotional agency (choice, flexibility, values-alignment)
summary: Learn to notice what you're feeling and respond in ways that actually work for you. It's about building real resilience through practice, not pretending emotions don't exist.

title: Getting Better at What Matters
tension: Repetitive grinding vs. adaptive growth | Passive consumption vs. directed struggle | Linear progression vs. non-linear plateaus
summary: Design practice that actually sticks by building feedback loops, moving through plateaus as growth moments, and stacking skills in the right order. Treat skill-building like a living system that adapts as you learn.

title: Getting Better When Perfect Isn't Possible
tension: Ideological purity vs. pragmatic progress | Perfect solutions vs. living with consequence
summary: Make progress toward justice through incremental steps when ideal solutions aren't available. Stay grounded in what actually works, stay accountable to people affected, and keep moving without compromising your values.

title: Getting Citizens to Shape City Decisions
tension: Deliberative legitimacy vs. Implementation reality — citizen participation generates binding decisions that bureaucracies cannot or will not execute, eroding trust in both participation and institutions.
summary: Help residents participate meaningfully in local governance while building the authority, skills, and engagement needed to make it work and keep it legitimate.

title: Getting Code Ready for Real People
tension: Speed of delivery vs. irreversibility of production harm; individual developer autonomy vs. collective system integrity
summary: Set up checks that catch problems before code goes live. Review what's being shipped, test it thoroughly, and make sure it actually works in production.

title: Getting Everyone Ready to Contribute
tension: Readiness (preparation, capability, alignment) vs. Momentum (urgency to begin, cost of delay, need to produce)
summary: Design rituals and checklists that prepare people before they take on real responsibility. This ensures new and experienced participants actually know what they're doing.

title: Getting Fresh Food to Your Neighborhood
tension: Centralization (efficiency, control, intermediation) vs. Decentralization (accessibility, autonomy, consent)
summary: Local food hubs and pickup points that connect nearby farmers with residents, using transit routes and shared spaces to make fresh food accessible without squeezing producers.

title: Getting Goods Around the City
tension: Centralized platform efficiency vs. distributed community resilience and worker agency
summary: Rethink how packages move through cities—from cargo bikes to shared distribution hubs—while using regulation and incentives to make delivery faster, cleaner, and fairer for everyone.

title: Getting Money Back When Things Go Wrong
tension: Speed & Fairness vs. Fraud Prevention & Financial Integrity
summary: When a payment fails or a mistake happens, the system needs to fix it fairly and fast—with clear reasons and a complete record of what occurred.

title: Getting Orders Right Every Step
tension: Speed of fulfillment vs. certainty of accuracy — moving goods fast while ensuring nothing reaches the customer wrong.
